summary: Sets out the requirements the Nimrod routing and addressing architecture places on the internetwork layer protocol, so that any protocol chosen as IPng supports it. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A wish list from one routing design saying what the new internet addresses must allow.

questions: what does ipng need for routing
subtitle: What the Nimrod routing architecture needs from the next-generation Internet Protocol.

tldr.problem: As the Internet grows, existing routing technologies won't scale adequately. Nimrod is a new routing and addressing architecture designed for a larger, more dynamic Internet.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents the technical requirements that any protocol chosen as IPng must satisfy to support Nimrod's design goals, covering packet format, fields, and how routing interacts with other network functions.
tldr.outcome: The document provides architectural guidance for IPng design. IPv6, ultimately adopted as IPng, incorporated many of these principles.

today: RFC 1753 is Informational and has not been updated or obsoleted. Its design principles influenced IPv6 (RFC 2460), which adopted many of the architectural concepts for future Internet scaling, though not all specific requirements.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC was submitted to the IETF's IPng area in response to the call for requirements from proposed routing and addressing architectures. It documents the technical requirements that the Nimrod routing and addressing architecture places on the internetwork layer protocol, in the hope that any protocol selected as IPng will satisfy these needs.

The author emphasizes that this document is specific to Nimrod, not a general statement of routing requirements. However, he argues that as routing technology evolves to meet the Internet's growing needs, fundamental principles will drive most large-scale routing architectures toward similar requirements.
sections.eli5: A group working on a new routing system called Nimrod wrote down what features they need the new Internet protocol to have.

sections.title: Packet Format Requirements
sections.content:
Nimrod requires that packets carry several pieces of information. Source and destination identification comes in three forms: globally unique identifiers (UIDs, at least 48 bits, recommended 64 bits), shorter endpoint selectors (ESELs) that map to unique values at each end, or inferred identification from setup information.

Packets must also carry flow identification to associate packets with longer-lived communications and their service requirements. For non-aggregated flows, a single flow-id field suffices; for aggregated flows, options include a sequence of flow-ids, a stack with the current one on top, or just the base and current flow-ids with router state at aggregation boundaries.

A looping packet detector (at least 12 bits, recommended 16 bits) must prevent packets stuck in the network. Optional source and destination locators (up to 32 bytes, recommended 256 bytes) are topologically sensitive identifiers. An optional pointer into locators helps prevent looping in datagram mode. Optional source routes support source-routed packet forwarding, requiring 512 bytes adequate, 2^16 recommended. An internetwork header length field must be at least 12 bits (16 recommended) since total headers could exceed 256 bytes.

Authentication and version number fields are also needed to support denial-of-service protection and future modifications to the header format.
sections.eli5: Packets need to carry address labels, flow tags, a hop counter to stop lost packets, and room for optional routing information—making the header bigger and more flexible than IPv4.

sections.title: Architectural Principles
sections.content:
Nimrod views the internetwork layer as a single distributed system composed of routing, resource allocation, security, and accounting subsystems. The design principle is "maximize the lifetime and flexibility of the architecture": optimizations that constrain future evolution should be avoided, even if they save space or performance today.

The document distinguishes between user state (what the user requests, such as destination addresses) and server state (longer-term information like resource allocations). Rather than forcing all user state into every packet, it should be installed in routers once, using a flow-id as the tag to find it. This reduces packet size and header overhead, especially for long-lived flows with complex requirements.

Nimrod's design recognizes that routers already contain state (routing tables) and argues that the critical difference from traditional datagram routing is mainly in the amount, granularity, and lifetime of state—not a fundamental architectural change.
sections.eli5: Instead of putting everything about a call into every packet, set up the router once with what you need, then each packet just says 'I belong to flow number 42.'

sections.title: Flows, State and Service Requirements
sections.content:
A flow, from the internetwork layer's perspective, is a sequence of packets that share all the attributes the network cares about: source and destination, path, resource allocation, accounting, authentication and security. Flows may be unicast or multicast; a single flow might contain multiple TCP connections, or a single application might span several flows (e.g., audio and video in a conference, each with different bandwidth needs).

The RFC identifies two schools of thought. The first holds that all user state should be repeated in each packet for robustness, with routers caching it for efficiency. The second argues that for flows generating many packets, setting up state in routers once—with a flow-id tag identifying it—is more efficient. This avoids repeating large amounts of information (source routes, resource requirements, security policies) in every header.

The architecture proposes a unified, system-wide flow mechanism rather than allowing each subsystem (routing, resource allocation, security, accounting) to define flows separately. This simplicity, the author argues, outweighs the flexibility of allowing multiple definitions.
sections.eli5: Packets that travel together can share the same instructions in the router, so we only tell the router once instead of repeating it in each packet.

sections.title: Requirements for the Internetwork Layer as a Whole
sections.content:
The RFC lists several requirements that IPng should provide to work well with Nimrod. These include a unified definition of flows and a flow-id field to identify them; a unified mechanism for setting up flow state in routers (including multicast flows); methods to learn whether a resource reservation succeeded along a path; support for multicast group membership; and multi-homing—the ability for a single endpoint to have multiple addresses and interfaces, with Nimrod decoupling transport identification (via endpoint identifiers) from interface identification (via locators).

Additional needs include support for multiple locators per interface, multiple endpoint identifiers per host, and distinction between a multicast group as a named entity and a multicast flow that may not reach all members. A distributed, replicated user name translation system (the RFC suggests DNS) must map user names into endpoint identifiers and locators.

These requirements reflect the view that IPng must support not just datagram delivery but also the control of flows, resource allocation, and the organizational structures needed for a global, large-scale Internet.
sections.eli5: The new protocol needs to let one computer have many addresses, let routers remember which packets belong together, and translate names to addresses quickly across the whole network.
